about: Interface rules for Relevo, written in its own words from the guidelines of UI UX Pro Max (see NOTICE and CURATION.md).

rules.title: Visible keyboard focus
rules.principle: Every control that can receive keyboard focus shows where the focus is, also inside a dialog or a sheet.
rules.ask: Is there a control whose focus the design hides or replaces?
rules.build: Keep a visible focus indicator on every interactive control; never remove the outline without a replacement.
rules.review: Tab through the screen and the open dialogs: the focused control is always visible.

rules.title: Text contrast
rules.principle: Text is readable against its background, in every theme the product ships. Body text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 (WCAG 1.4.3, level AA); large text needs 3:1.
rules.ask: Which text sits on a coloured, image or dark-mode background?
rules.build: Pick text and background pairs from the design tokens and check the ratio of each pair, in light and dark.
rules.review: Measure the ratio of body, secondary and disabled-looking text in each theme; flag any pair under 4.5:1.

rules.title: Meaning is not carried by colour alone
rules.principle: A state, an error or a category is also given by an icon, a shape or text, so a person who cannot tell the colours apart gets it (WCAG 1.4.1).
rules.ask: What states or categories does the design show only with a colour?
rules.build: Add an icon or a word to every state that is coloured: error, success, selected, required.
rules.review: Look at the screen in greyscale: every state is still told apart.

examples.good: Red text with an error icon and the word "Error"
examples.bad: Only a red border marks the error

rules.title: Text alternatives for images
rules.principle: An image that carries meaning has a text alternative that says what it shows; a decorative one is hidden from assistive technology (WCAG 1.1.1).
rules.ask: Which images carry information, and which are decoration?
rules.build: Give each meaningful image a short description; mark decorative images as decorative.
rules.review: Every meaningful image has a description; no image has a filename or "image" as its description.

examples.good: Semantics(label: 'A dog playing in a park', child: Image.asset('dog.jpg'))

rules.title: Headings follow a sequence
rules.principle: Headings are used in order, without skipping levels, because screen reader users move through a page by its headings (WCAG 1.3.1).
rules.ask: What are the sections of the page and how are they nested?
rules.build: Use one h1 and the next level for each subsection; style headings with CSS, not by choosing a level.
rules.review: The heading levels read as an outline with no skipped level.

rules.title: Every control has an accessible name
rules.principle: A control that has no visible text, such as an icon button, still has a name that a screen reader announces (WCAG 4.1.2).
rules.ask: Which controls show only an icon?
rules.build: Give every icon-only control a name in the language of the product.
rules.review: Each icon-only button has a name; the name says the action, not the icon.

examples.good: IconButton(tooltip: 'Close menu', icon: Icon(Icons.close), onPressed: close)
examples.bad: IconButton(icon: Icon(Icons.close), onPressed: close)  // no tooltip or label

rules.title: Everything works with the keyboard
rules.principle: Every action that a pointer can do can be done with the keyboard, in an order that follows the visual order (WCAG 2.1.1).
rules.ask: Which interactions depend on hover, drag or a custom control?
rules.build: Use native controls; keep the tab order the same as the visual order; give custom controls the keys people expect.
rules.review: Do each action of the change with the keyboard alone, with no unreachable element.

rules.title: Use the semantics of the platform
rules.principle: Structure is expressed with the elements the platform provides (landmarks, lists, buttons), so assistive technology can read it.
rules.ask: What regions does the page have: navigation, main content, side content?
rules.build: Use native structure elements before generic containers with a role added.
rules.review: The page has a main region and its navigation is a navigation element, not a stack of generic containers.

rules.title: Inputs have a visible label
rules.principle: Every input has a label that stays visible and is tied to it in code; a placeholder is a hint, not a label (WCAG 3.3.2, 1.3.1).
rules.ask: Does every field have a label that stays on screen while the person types?
rules.build: Put a label above or beside each input and associate it with the input.
rules.review: Clicking or reading the label reaches its input; no field relies on a placeholder as its only label.

rules.title: Errors are announced
rules.principle: An error appears in a way that assistive technology announces, not only on screen (WCAG 4.1.3).
rules.ask: Where does an error appear and how would a screen reader user learn of it?
rules.build: Mark the error message so that it is announced when it appears, and tie it to its field.
rules.review: Trigger an error with a screen reader or inspect the markup: the message is announced and tied to the field.

examples.good: Semantics(liveRegion: true, child: Text('Enter a valid email'))
examples.bad: Text shown in red with no live region

rules.title: A way to skip repeated navigation
rules.principle: A keyboard user can jump past the repeated header to the main content (WCAG 2.4.1).
rules.ask: Does the page repeat a long header or menu before the content?
rules.build: Add a first link that moves focus to the main content.
rules.review: The first Tab stop is a link to the main content, and it works.

examples.good: Skip to main content
examples.bad: A header with dozens of links before the content

rules.title: Focus is not hidden behind other content
rules.principle: A focused control is not entirely hidden by a sticky header, a banner or another persistent layer (WCAG 2.4.11, level AA). Keeping it at least partly visible is the safer reading.
rules.ask: Which elements stay fixed on screen while the page scrolls?
rules.build: Leave room for fixed elements with scroll padding, or move or dismiss a persistent layer when focus goes under it.
rules.review: Tab through the page with a fixed header and banner open: no focused control is entirely hidden, and ideally none is even partly covered.

examples.bad: A fixed bar that covers the focused control

rules.title: Dragging has a single-pointer alternative
rules.principle: Anything that can be done by dragging can also be done with a tap or a click and the keyboard (WCAG 2.5.7, level AA).
rules.ask: Which interactions need a drag: reorder, resize, slide?
rules.build: Add buttons or a menu next to the drag handle, such as move up and move down.
rules.review: Reorder or move an item without dragging: buttons, menu or keyboard.

examples.good: Move up and Move down buttons beside the drag handle
examples.bad: A drag handle as the only way to reorder

rules.title: Pointer targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels
rules.principle: A target a pointer must hit is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or has enough spacing, unless an exception applies (WCAG 2.5.8, level AA).
rules.ask: Which controls are small or close together: icon buttons, inline links, table actions?
rules.build: Make controls at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels or space them so each has a 24-pixel circle that touches no other target.
rules.review: Measure the smallest control of the change at the narrowest width; check adjacent icon buttons.

examples.bad: Tiny icon buttons side by side

rules.title: Signing in does not need a memory or puzzle test
rules.principle: Signing in does not rely only on remembering, transcribing or solving something; password managers and paste work, or another method is offered (WCAG 3.3.8, level AA).
rules.ask: How does a person sign in or confirm identity: a password, a code, a puzzle?
rules.build: Let password managers fill the field, allow paste, and offer another way such as a passkey or a sign-in link.
rules.review: Paste into the password field works; the field has the right autocomplete value.

rules.title: Auto-moving content can be stopped
rules.principle: Content that moves, blinks or updates by itself for more than five seconds, next to other content, has a way to pause, stop or hide it (WCAG 2.2.2). As good practice it also stops while the person focuses it and when they ask for less motion.
rules.ask: Does anything advance or animate without the person asking?
rules.build: Add previous, next and pause controls; stop while focused or hovered; stop when reduced motion is requested.
rules.review: Find any auto-advancing content: it has a pause control and honours the reduced-motion setting.

examples.bad: A carousel that advances on a timer with no control

rules.title: A failed form offers an error summary
rules.principle: After a failed submit, a summary at the top lists the problems, takes focus, and links to each invalid field, next to the error beside each field. The inline error is what WCAG 3.3.1 asks for; the summary is a technique that makes the errors easy to find.
rules.ask: How does a person find out which fields failed after they submit?
rules.build: Show a summary at the top that receives focus after a failed submit; link each item to its field; keep the inline errors.
rules.review: Submit an invalid form: focus lands on the summary and each item reaches its field.

examples.good:
There is a problem

Enter an email
examples.bad: A toast with no links and no focus target

rules.title: Text reflows and survives user spacing
rules.principle: Text stays readable at a narrow width, at 200% zoom and when the person overrides spacing: no horizontal scrolling, no clipped text (WCAG 1.4.4, 1.4.10, 1.4.12).
rules.ask: Is any text in a box with a fixed height or width?
rules.build: Use fluid sizes, heights that follow the content and a unitless line height.
rules.review: Zoom to 200% and narrow the window to 320 CSS pixels: no text is cut off and nothing scrolls sideways.

rules.title: Chips and toggles are real controls
rules.principle: A chip that can be selected has a native role, a name, a state, keyboard operation and visible focus.
rules.ask: Are there filters or toggles drawn as chips or pills?
rules.build: Use a button that exposes its pressed or selected state, and make the state match the visible label.
rules.review: A chip is a button with a pressed or selected state; a clickable div is not accepted.

rules.title: Changing counts are announced in context
rules.principle: When a count or badge changes without the person acting on it, a short status message tells them what changed, without moving focus.
rules.ask: What counts or badges update after load?
rules.build: Announce one complete message, such as "3 items in cart", through a status region.
rules.review: Change the count and listen or inspect: one complete message, no change of focus.

rules.title: Layers use a defined scale
rules.principle: Stacking order comes from a small shared scale, and a new stacking context is understood before a bigger number is tried.
rules.ask: Which elements overlap: menus, dialogs, toasts, sticky bars?
rules.build: Use the layer values of the design system; do not raise a number to win a conflict.
rules.review: No new arbitrary huge layer value; overlapping elements stack in the intended order.

rules.title: Clipping does not hide content
rules.principle: A container that clips its content must not hide anything the person needs.
rules.ask: Which containers have a fixed size and long or variable content?
rules.build: Let a container scroll or grow before clipping; test it with the longest content.
rules.review: Fill each container with the longest realistic content: nothing needed is cut off.

rules.title: Fixed elements leave room for each other
rules.principle: Fixed bars, banners and safe areas are accounted for so they do not cover content or each other.
rules.ask: Which elements are fixed to the screen edges?
rules.build: Reserve space for fixed elements and the safe area; keep a gap between fixed bars.
rules.review: Scroll to the end of the page on a small screen: the last content is reachable and no fixed element covers another.

examples.good: A fixed top bar and a fixed bottom bar with padding for both

rules.title: Late content does not move the layout
rules.principle: Images, badges, validation text and replaced skeletons reserve their space so the content around them does not jump when they appear.
rules.ask: What appears after the first paint: images, counts, messages?
rules.build: Reserve space with an aspect ratio, a fixed slot or a skeleton of the same size.
rules.review: Reload with a slow network: nothing near the late content moves when it arrives.

examples.bad: An image with no size that pushes the text down

examples.good: A slot of stable size for a count badge
examples.bad: A badge whose insertion pushes the toolbar actions

rules.title: Full-height layouts account for browser chrome on phones
rules.principle: A full-screen section is sized for the visible area on a phone, whose address bar changes the viewport.
rules.ask: Is a section meant to fill the screen?
rules.build: Use the dynamic viewport units where they are supported.
rules.review: Open on a phone-sized viewport: the section fits without a part hidden behind the browser bar.

rules.title: Checked at the common widths
rules.principle: A layout is checked at the widths people use, not only at the developer screen.
rules.ask: Which widths must the page support?
rules.build: Build mobile first and verify at 320, 375, 414, 768, 1024 and 1440 CSS pixels.
rules.review: Open the change at 320, 375, 768, 1024 and 1440 pixels: nothing breaks.

examples.bad: Developed and checked at one screen size

rules.title: Small screens get touch-sized controls
rules.principle: On a small screen the controls are big enough for a finger, even if the desktop version is compact.
rules.ask: Which controls are used on a phone?
rules.build: Increase the size and spacing of controls on small screens.
rules.review: Tap each control at 360 pixels wide: none is hard to hit.

examples.good: Larger buttons below the medium breakpoint

rules.title: Body text is readable on every device
rules.principle: Body text is large enough to read without zooming. On the web about 16 CSS pixels (1rem) is the usual floor for body text on a phone, a convention and not a standard; on iOS the default text size is 17 pt and the minimum 11 pt (Apple Human Interface Guidelines).
rules.ask: What size is the smallest text a person must read?
rules.build: Use at least the base size for body text; reserve smaller sizes for secondary labels.
rules.review: Body text is not below the base size at 360 pixels wide; text respects the text size the person set.

examples.good: text-base or larger for body text
Theme text styles with the default body size, scaled by the system text scale

rules.title: Pages declare the viewport
rules.principle: A web page tells the browser to use the device width, or it is shown as a shrunken desktop page on a phone.
rules.ask: Is this a new page or a new HTML entry?
rules.build: Include the viewport declaration in the document head.
rules.review: The head has a viewport declaration with the device width and no zoom lock.

rules.title: No sideways scrolling of the page
rules.principle: The page fits the width of the viewport; only a component meant to scroll, such as a wide table, scrolls sideways.
rules.ask: Is any element wider than a phone screen?
rules.build: Constrain widths to the viewport; let wide content scroll inside its own container.
rules.review: Open at 320 and 360 pixels: the page has no horizontal scrollbar.

examples.bad: A fixed-width element that causes a horizontal scrollbar

rules.title: Images scale with their container
rules.principle: Images shrink with their container instead of overflowing it.
rules.ask: Which images are placed in flexible containers?
rules.build: Give images a maximum width of their container and an automatic height.
rules.review: No image is wider than its container at 320 pixels.

rules.title: Tables work on small screens
rules.principle: A table either scrolls inside its own container or turns into a list of cards on a narrow screen.
rules.ask: Does the change add a table with many columns?
rules.build: Wrap the table in a scroll container or switch to a card layout at small widths.
rules.review: Open the table at 360 pixels: it does not push the page wider.

examples.good: A wrapper with overflow-x-auto around the table
examples.bad: A table that overflows the viewport

rules.title: Long content is cut gracefully
rules.principle: Long text is shortened with an ellipsis where space is limited, and the full text stays reachable.
rules.ask: Which texts can be longer than the space for them?
rules.build: Clamp the lines and offer a way to see the rest.
rules.review: Use the longest realistic title: it is clamped and the full text is reachable.

examples.bad: Text that is cut off with no way to read it

rules.title: Long words and identifiers wrap
rules.principle: URLs, identifiers and user-written text must not force the layout wider than its container.
rules.ask: Which fields show user-written text or long identifiers?
rules.build: Allow breaks inside long tokens and let text children of flex or grid items shrink.
rules.review: Paste a 60-character word without spaces in each text field: the layout does not overflow.

rules.title: Essential text is never lost to truncation
rules.principle: Headings, action labels, error messages, safety text and the names that tell items apart are shown completely, or a visible way to read them in full is provided.
rules.ask: Which texts are essential to understand or act?
rules.build: Let essential text wrap, stack or resize; offer a visible full-detail path if it must be shortened.
rules.review: Increase the text size and use long labels: no action or error is reduced to an unexplained ellipsis.

examples.good: An action label that wraps or opens full details
examples.bad: A primary action shown only as an unexplained ellipsis

rules.title: A badge states, a chip acts
rules.principle: A badge communicates a state and is not interactive; a chip stands for a value or an action and is a control. The markup follows the meaning.
rules.ask: Is each small label a state, a value or an action?
rules.build: Use static markup for a state; use a control for anything that can be pressed or removed.
rules.review: A pressable pill is a control; a plain status label has no click handler.

rules.title: Chip collections keep their labels
rules.principle: A set of filter or value chips wraps, or offers a working "+n" control for hidden values; it does not clip a chip when space or text size changes.
rules.ask: How many chips can there be and how long are their labels?
rules.build: Wrap the collection, or hide the overflow behind an operable "+n" disclosure.
rules.review: Add many chips and increase the text size: none is silently cut off.

rules.title: Short labels stay whole and disclose cuts
rules.principle: A badge, chip or pill label stays on one line when it can, bounds only values that are unpredictable, and shows the full value to keyboard, pointer and touch users when it must be cut.
rules.ask: Can a label be longer than its pill?
rules.build: Let the label shrink, keep it on one line, and give an operable way to see the full value.
rules.review: Use a long label: it is cut only if needed, and the full value is reachable without a hover.

examples.good: A flexible label with a minimum width of zero and a disclosure of the full value
examples.bad: A fixed-width badge that wraps or clips with a title tooltip as its only recovery

rules.title: Each invalid field shows its own error
rules.principle: An invalid field has a specific message next to it, tied to the field in code.
rules.ask: What can be wrong in each field and what should the message say?
rules.build: Show a specific message under the field and connect it to the input.
rules.review: Each invalid field has its own message that says what to fix and is tied to the input.

examples.bad: A red border or a summary only

examples.good: TextFormField(validator: (v) => v!.isEmpty ? 'Enter an email address' : null)
examples.bad: A red border with no message

rules.title: Validate when a person leaves the field
rules.principle: Most fields are checked when the person leaves them, not on every key and not only at submit.
rules.ask: When should each field report a problem?
rules.build: Validate on blur, and again on submit.
rules.review: Fill a field wrongly and leave it: the message appears then, not while typing.

rules.title: Use the input type that matches the data
rules.principle: An email, phone number or number field uses the matching input type so the platform offers the right keyboard and checks.
rules.ask: What kind of data does each field take?
rules.build: Pick the specific input type for each field.
rules.review: Email, phone and numeric fields do not use a generic text type.

rules.title: Let the browser fill known fields
rules.principle: Fields that ask for known personal data declare what they are, so autofill and password managers work and the purpose of the field can be determined by software (WCAG 1.3.5, level AA).
rules.ask: Which fields ask for a name, an address, an email or a password?
rules.build: Set the autocomplete value that matches each field; do not switch it off everywhere.
rules.review: Name, email and address fields declare their autocomplete value.

rules.title: Required fields are marked
rules.principle: A person can tell which fields are required before they submit.
rules.ask: Which fields are required?
rules.build: Mark required fields with a symbol that is explained, or the word "required".
rules.review: The form says which fields are required.

examples.good: An asterisk with a note "* required"
examples.bad: No marking; the person must guess

rules.title: A password can be shown
rules.principle: A person can reveal what they typed in a password field to avoid mistakes.
rules.ask: Is there a password field?
rules.build: Add a show or hide control with an accessible name.
rules.review: The password field has a toggle that changes the visibility and announces its state.

examples.bad: A password that is always hidden

rules.title: A submit shows what happened
rules.principle: After a submit the person sees that it is in progress, then that it worked or failed.
rules.ask: What does the person see between pressing submit and the result?
rules.build: Show a busy state, then a success or an error message.
rules.review: Submit with a slow and with a failing request: the person is told what happened each time.

examples.good: Loading, then a success or error message
examples.bad: A button that does nothing visible after a click

rules.title: The keyboard matches the field
rules.principle: On a phone the keyboard that opens suits the data: digits for a number, an email keyboard for an address.
rules.ask: Which fields expect numbers or an email?
rules.build: Choose the keyboard type for each field.
rules.review: On a device, a numeric field opens the numeric keyboard.

examples.bad: A text keyboard for a number
The default keyboard for a number

rules.title: Primary actions do not depend on hover
rules.principle: Hover does not exist on touch devices, so anything important is reachable by click or tap and by keyboard.
rules.ask: Does anything appear only when the pointer rests on it?
rules.build: Use click, tap or focus for primary interactions; use hover only as an extra.
rules.review: The change works on a touch device and with the keyboard; no action is available only on hover.

examples.good: An onClick handler for the menu
examples.bad: A menu that opens only on mouse enter

rules.title: Controls respond when pressed
rules.principle: A control gives immediate feedback when pressed.
rules.ask: Which controls are pressed or clicked?
rules.build: Give pressed controls a visible change.
rules.review: Press a button: something visibly changes right away.

rules.title: Disabled looks disabled
rules.principle: A control that cannot be used looks different from one that can, and says why when that is not obvious.
rules.ask: When is each control unavailable?
rules.build: Reduce emphasis and show a not-allowed cursor; explain the reason where it is not clear.
rules.review: A disabled control is distinct from an enabled one and keeps its text readable.

examples.bad: The same style as the enabled control

rules.title: Async actions cannot be sent twice
rules.principle: While an action is running its control cannot start it again, and it shows that it is busy.
rules.ask: Which actions take time and change data?
rules.build: Disable the control and show a busy state until the action ends.
rules.review: Press an async action twice quickly: the second press does nothing.

examples.bad: onPressed: save  // while the request is running

rules.title: A failure is shown where it happened
rules.principle: When something fails the person is told, near the problem, in plain words.
rules.ask: What can fail and what should the person do?
rules.build: Show a clear message close to what failed, with a next step.
rules.review: Make the request fail: a message appears near the cause, and it says what to do.

examples.good: A red border with a message that says what to fix

rules.title: A success is confirmed
rules.principle: A completed action is confirmed with a short message or a visible change.
rules.ask: How does the person know that an action worked?
rules.build: Show a brief confirmation or an obvious state change.
rules.review: Complete the action: something confirms it.

examples.good: A toast or a check mark after saving

rules.title: Destructive actions are confirmed
rules.principle: An action that deletes or cannot be undone asks for confirmation, or can be undone.
rules.ask: Which actions delete data or cannot be reversed?
rules.build: Ask for confirmation that names what will be lost, or offer an undo.
rules.review: Trigger each destructive action: it asks first or can be undone.

examples.good: A dialog that says "Delete this report?" with a clear confirm

rules.title: Durations come from shared tokens
rules.principle: Motion lasts as long as the distance and the task need, from shared values, and feedback stays quick.
rules.ask: Which things move and how far?
rules.build: Use the motion tokens of the project; keep feedback short.
rules.review: Animations use shared durations, not one value copied everywhere.

examples.bad: One duration pasted into every transition

rules.title: Reduced motion is respected
rules.principle: When the person asks the system for less motion, animation is reduced and parallax or scroll-driven effects show the final readable state. This is a platform preference, not a level of a standard.
rules.ask: Which animations are not essential?
rules.build: Check the reduced-motion setting and replace movement with a state change or a fade.
rules.review: Turn on reduced motion: large movement and parallax stop, and the content is still readable.

rules.title: Endless animation is for loading only
rules.principle: Looping animation distracts; it is kept for indicators of a wait.
rules.ask: Does anything animate forever?
rules.build: Loop only a loading indicator.
rules.review: No decorative element animates continuously.

rules.title: Animate cheap properties
rules.principle: Animating transform and opacity is smooth; animating layout properties is not.
rules.ask: Which properties will an animation change?
rules.build: Animate transform and opacity.
rules.review: No animation changes top, left, width or height.

rules.title: Transitions can be interrupted
rules.principle: If the person acts again while a transition runs, the earlier motion is cancelled and the final state is set directly; the state never waits for an animation to end.
rules.ask: Can a control be changed again before its animation finishes?
rules.build: Cancel or replace the previous motion and set the new state at once.
rules.review: Click a toggle quickly several times: the final state is the last one clicked.

examples.bad: Enabling the state only inside a transitionend handler

rules.title: Waiting is shown without flicker
rules.principle: A wait shows feedback that suits its length: nothing for instant work, a stable placeholder or progress for longer, with the layout and focus kept and a busy status for assistive technology.
rules.ask: How long can this wait be and what is on screen meanwhile?
rules.build: Keep the layout stable with a placeholder or a progress indicator; mark the region as busy.
rules.review: Throttle the network: a stable placeholder appears, the layout does not jump, nothing flashes for a fast response.

examples.bad: A blank screen or a spinner that flashes

examples.good: A placeholder of the final size while the future resolves

rules.title: An empty list helps
rules.principle: When there is nothing to show, the screen says why and offers the next action.
rules.ask: What does the screen show when there is no data?
rules.build: Show a short explanation and an action.
rules.review: Empty the list: a message and an action appear, not blank space.

rules.title: An error offers a way forward
rules.principle: An error message says what the person can do next.
rules.ask: What can the person do after each failure?
rules.build: Offer a retry or a help path with the message.
rules.review: Each error has a next step.

examples.good: A message with a "Try again" button

rules.title: Multi-step flows show progress
rules.principle: A process in several steps shows where the person is and how many steps remain.
rules.ask: How many steps does the flow have?
rules.build: Show the current step and the total.
rules.review: A multi-step flow shows its position.

rules.title: Transient messages are for non-critical news
rules.principle: A message that disappears is for information that is not critical; anything the person must act on stays.
rules.ask: Does a message carry something the person must not miss?
rules.build: Auto-dismiss only non-critical messages after a few seconds.
rules.review: A critical message does not disappear by itself.

examples.good: A toast that dismisses after 4 seconds for "Saved"
examples.bad: A persistent toast for routine news

rules.title: Body text has room between lines
rules.principle: Body text is easier to read with a line height of about 1.5 to 1.75.
rules.ask: What text is set in long paragraphs?
rules.build: Set body line height around 1.5.
rules.review: Body paragraphs are not set tighter than 1.4.

rules.title: Lines are not too long
rules.principle: Long text is limited to roughly 65 to 75 characters per line, the usual target; WCAG 1.4.8 (level AAA, so enhanced) allows at most 80. This also limits the width of text containers.
rules.ask: Which text runs the full width of a wide screen?
rules.build: Limit the width of reading text.
rules.review: At 1440 pixels the paragraphs are not wider than about 75 characters.

rules.title: Sizes come from a scale
rules.principle: Text sizes come from one scale, so the hierarchy is consistent.
rules.ask: Which text sizes does the screen need?
rules.build: Use the sizes of the type scale of the design system.
rules.review: No new arbitrary font size is introduced.

rules.title: Fonts load without shifting the page
rules.principle: A web font appears without blocking the text or moving the layout: a fallback of similar size is shown first.
rules.ask: Does the change add a font?
rules.build: Use a swap or optional display and a fallback with similar metrics.
rules.review: Reload with a slow network: the text is visible at once and does not jump when the font loads.

examples.bad: A web font with no fallback and invisible text while it loads

rules.title: Images are the right size and format
rules.principle: An image is served at about the size it is shown, in a modern format.
rules.ask: Which images are large or photographic?
rules.build: Provide sizes for different screens and a compressed format.
rules.review: No very large image is used for a small slot.

rules.title: Below-the-fold content loads when needed
rules.principle: Content that is not visible at first loads later.
rules.ask: What is below the first screen?
rules.build: Lazy load below-the-fold images and heavy content.
rules.review: Only the first screen of images loads eagerly.

rules.title: Large code loads by route
rules.principle: A large piece of code that only one route needs is loaded for that route.
rules.ask: Does the change add a heavy library?
rules.build: Load route-specific code on demand.
rules.review: A heavy dependency for one route is imported lazily.

examples.bad: import Chart from './Chart.vue' in the main bundle

rules.title: External scripts do not block rendering
rules.principle: Scripts the page does not need to render load without blocking it.
rules.ask: Does the change add an external script?
rules.build: Load non-critical scripts with async or defer.
rules.review: No external script blocks the head.

rules.title: A fixed header does not cover content
rules.principle: Content starts below a fixed navigation bar.
rules.ask: Is the navigation fixed to the top?
rules.build: Offset the content by the height of the bar.
rules.review: The first section is not hidden under the bar.

rules.title: The current place is marked
rules.principle: Navigation shows where the person is, in a way that is not only a colour.
rules.ask: Which item is current?
rules.build: Mark the active item with an underline or weight as well as colour, and with an accessible current state.
rules.review: The current item is distinguishable.

examples.good: border-b-2 text-primary on the active item

rules.title: Back goes where people expect
rules.principle: The back action returns to the previous place; navigation history is kept.
rules.ask: Which steps push a new place on the history?
rules.build: Push routes that the person would go back from; do not replace them.
rules.review: Back returns to the previous screen from each flow.

examples.bad: location.replace() for a view people go back from
Navigator.pushReplacement for a screen people go back from

rules.title: The address reflects the view
rules.principle: A view that can be shared or reloaded has an address that reproduces it.
rules.ask: Which states should survive a reload or a shared link?
rules.build: Reflect filters, tabs and selected items in the URL or route.
rules.review: Reload the page: the same view returns.

examples.bad: A single address for every state

rules.title: Dates follow the locale
rules.principle: Dates are shown in a form the person reads easily, using the locale.
rules.ask: Which dates are displayed?
rules.build: Format dates with the locale; use relative dates when that helps.
rules.review: No hand-built date strings.

examples.good: "2 hours ago" or a locale format

rules.title: Numbers are readable
rules.principle: Large numbers use separators or abbreviations.
rules.ask: Which numbers are large?
rules.build: Format numbers with the locale.
rules.review: No raw long numbers.

rules.title: Sample content is realistic
rules.principle: Sample data looks like real data so layout problems show up early.
rules.ask: What sample content is used while building?
rules.build: Use realistic names, lengths and values.
rules.review: No lorem ipsum left in the change.

rules.title: Touch targets are large enough
rules.principle: A target for a finger is at least 48 dp on Android (Android Developers) and 44 by 44 pt on iOS (Apple Human Interface Guidelines); the web has its own rule.
rules.ask: Which controls are small?
rules.build: Size touch targets to the platform guideline, even when the icon is smaller.
rules.review: Measure the smallest control of the change; none is below the platform size.

examples.good: IconButton with the default 48 dp constraints
44 pt on iOS and 48 dp on Android

rules.title: Touch targets are spaced apart
rules.principle: Neighbouring targets have a gap so the wrong one is not pressed.
rules.ask: Which controls sit next to each other?
rules.build: Leave at least 8 px between touch targets.
rules.review: Adjacent controls have a visible gap.

rules.title: Custom gestures do not fight the system
rules.principle: Custom gestures do not collide with scrolling or the system gestures.
rules.ask: Does the change add a swipe?
rules.build: Keep vertical scroll primary; avoid a main-content horizontal swipe as the only way.
rules.review: On a device, scroll and system back still work.

examples.good: Vertical scroll with buttons for sideways moves
examples.bad: A horizontal swipe as the only navigation

rules.title: Search helps while typing
rules.principle: Predictions appear as the person types.
rules.ask: Is there a search field with a large set of results?
rules.build: Show debounced suggestions.
rules.review: Typing shows suggestions without a request per key.

examples.good: A debounced request and a list of suggestions

rules.title: No results offers a way on
rules.principle: An empty result says so and suggests what to do next.
rules.ask: What happens when a search finds nothing?
rules.build: Explain and suggest another search or action.
rules.review: A search with no results shows a helpful message.

examples.good: "No results for X. Try a shorter word."

rules.title: Media does not start by itself
rules.principle: Video and audio start when the person asks, with a pause control and captions.
rules.ask: Does the change play media?
rules.build: Prefer click to play; add captions; stop off-screen and honour reduced motion.
rules.review: No media starts on its own.
